item.title: You Can Make Luck Happen
item.description:
Positive Psychology

You Can Make Luck Happen

The open-minded enjoy luck 运气 for a reason.

Posted October 14, 2026

Key points
  • The lucky have their eyes peeled for fortune and happy accidents around every corner.
  • People who feel cursed, like the person who never gets a leg up, create negative self-fulfilling prophecies.

When we stay open to life’s potential, we may experience luck 运气. Luck can be useful in the quest for positivity. Lucky people are flexible, hopeful, resilient, and open; they mine new opportunities for their own gain and have their eyes peeled for fortune and happy accidents around every corner. Can we be more open to luck?

From their youth, my parents remembered villagers in their homeland panning for gold in a nearby river. Those who panned and hit the jackpot were considered the town’s luckiest. A neighbor was one such charmed soul. He was walking by the river when he stopped to gulp some water. On his knees, he saw a glint that begged for a closer look. A rock covered most of that shiny something; the neighbor moved it and found several gold nuggets, each the size of his thumb. He pocketed these precious lumps and ran home. He didn’t squander away the gold on frivolous material goods. Instead, his windfall afforded him and his kin a house, half a mountain, chickens, and goats. He was so lucky.

Source: AI-Assisted

Luck sticks to certain people, and not others. The inherently unlucky seem to walk around inviting misfortune. It makes me wonder why kismet keeps finding the lucky ones again and again.

I like to think the lucky ones are open-minded. We make our own luck, argues Richard Wiseman, a psychology professor at the University of Hertfordshire in the United Kingdom and author of The Luck Factor. He notes that we can learn to be curious and lucky in different ways—creating opportunities, feeling lucky, expecting luck to appear wherever and whenever, and seeing the good in the bad. In truth, the lucky are mindful, tolerant, and aware of life’s possibilities. Essentially, the lucky are not mired in negative thinking.

Those who invite good karma are skilled at moving on to the next thing when fortune isn’t showing itself. Sometimes you can’t get that dream job because someone else occupies the seat; therefore, a mental pivot may be required.

Plus, people open to fortune are also open to risk; this is a useful trait if you want to experience life more fully. They have an “I Can Win” quality. Meanwhile, the unlucky often lament how life offers them no miracles of positive karma. Wiseman noted that those who feel cursed, like the person who thinks he is never given a leg up, create self-fulfilling prophecies. You think something will happen, and it will happen: I’m not lucky, and I never will be.

People who experience luck early in life may expect and look for open doors later in life. Meanwhile, those who do not experience good karma early don’t know any better. To put it simply, good tidings beget future good tidings. This is similar to “The Matthew Effect,” which was a term coined in the late 1960s by sociologists Robert Merton and Harriet Zuckerman. The phenomenon is named after the Bible’s Parable of the Talents or Minas in the Gospel of Matthew. This concept acknowledges the advantages of people who are born with more resources. In simple terms, the rich stay rich, so to speak. This also subtly applies to the luck phenomenon. The lucky stay lucky—or at least they think that way.

A Most Amazing Story of Kismet

The most amazing story of luck I know involves my parents during the Chinese Communist Revolution. When Mao Zedong’s revolution marched toward their province in the mid-20th century, the people were frantic. The wealthy and educated tried to flee.

My dad could not secure passage out of the country, but he was educated and worked for the government, so he was in danger. At the very least, my dad was determined to get his family on the plane, which he did. He was left behind.

As an English speaker, he was called upon to translate for visiting foreigners. One was Lieutenant General Claire Lee Chennault, the founder of the Flying Tigers, the First American Volunteer Group of the Republic of China Air Force. My dad had helped Chennault negotiate an airstrip in our hometown. Chennault said to him, “If the Communists catch you, you’re a dead man.” The general told my dad to hide in a pile of lamb’s wool and wait. He hid for three days until Chennault ordered an incoming pilot to whisk Dad away.

What luck.

Meanwhile, my mother thought that she would never see him again and that he would surely die in China. After she and her family arrived in Guangdong, she was puffy-eyed and grief-stricken as she sat on a bench with her mother, watching refugees moving in and out of an elevator. When the elevator opened and closed, she was sure she had glimpsed her husband; at six feet, he was taller than the average Chinaman.

“I think I just saw my husband,” she said, tugging Grandma’s sleeve.

Grandma shook her head. “You’re crying so much that you’re seeing things now.”

A few minutes later, the elevator opened again, and out walked Dad.

I think Dad was lucky because he believed he was, which made him open to looking around and seeing life’s possibilities. I want to be lucky like he was.

item.title: Do You Seek Validation Because of Low Self-Esteem?
item.description:
Self-Esteem

Do You Seek Validation Because of Low Self-Esteem?

If your self-esteem is lacking, you might need validation just to feel OK.

Posted October 14, 2026

Key points
  • Seeking validation is a normal, healthy human need.
  • But if your self-esteem is shaky, you may crave validation more than most.
  • Learning to love and validate yourself is always possible, with the right help and support.
Source: George Pagan III/Unsplash

We all need validation. Especially as children developing our sense of self, we need validation from our parents to build confidence and self-worth. Sadly, many of my clients didn’t receive enough validation when they were young, so now they struggle with low self-esteem.

If we worked hard on a school project, we needed to be told, “Well done! I’m so proud of you.” Crucially, not because we got an A for our project, but because we worked hard and did our best. Many parents, especially narcissistic ones, give praise only when their kids achieve highly.

That’s because narcissistic mums and dads see their kids as extensions of themselves. Their children’s success is their success. And their failures are also perceived to be a reflection of the self-involved parent, which triggers shame—an emotion that is unbearable for narcissistic folks.

If this is ringing bells for you, I’m sorry. It’s incredibly hard to grow up with this kind of parenting, because it progressively erodes your self-esteem, making you anxious and desperate for the tiny crumbs of praise and appreciation that come your way.

A Deep-Seated Hunger for Approval

Another thing I often see in my consulting room is people whose parents were too demanding, too pushy. Nothing was ever good enough for these hard taskmasters, making my clients feel worthless and like they could never measure up, no matter how hard they tried.

If your parent was like this, you may have internalized these overly demanding messages—“Try harder!” or “Why can’t you be more like your sister? She’s so much smarter than you”—and now that messaging is internal, communicated by your inner critic.

Let’s examine this craving for approval through Debbie’s story. Debbie* came to see me because her self-esteem was at rock bottom. She had just been made redundant from her job, her relationship felt stagnant, and Debbie was worried her boyfriend was losing interest. Putting her job situation to one side for the moment, we focused on how she behaved in her relationship.

“I get really needy,” she admitted. “When Dave seems bored or disinterested, I try to get his attention and start fishing for compliments, asking if he finds me attractive or likes the new dress I’m wearing. I know it seems really shallow and I kind of hate myself for it, but I just can’t seem to stop.”

Little Debbie’s Yearning for Love

I reassured Debbie that it didn’t seem needy at all. She was at a low ebb, having just lost her job. And her boyfriend was often distracted, staring at his phone for hours. This lack of interest, feeling unseen and unheard, was painfully familiar to Debbie, because her mother was an alcoholic, drinking heavily every day throughout Debbie’s childhood.

“She was always bombed,” recalled Debbie tearfully. “I remember showing her a picture I drew of her at school, feeling really proud and hoping she would like it. But she was drunk, as usual, and spilled her drink all over it before laughing and staggering away. I felt crushed, but I kept drawing her pictures, hoping each time she would be happy, but she never was.”

Viewed through a schema therapy lens, poor Debbie’s normal, healthy needs for love and to be valued were profoundly unmet. Because this stressful event occurred over and over when she was young, she developed painful schemas in her brain, which are templates for how to respond to adverse events like these. Her defectiveness schema contained beliefs about being unlovable and unimportant, while an approval-seeking schema also developed, which was compensatory for the first schema. If she sought—and received—approval, this helped her feel a little better, numbing out the pain of that sense of being defective. As an adult, every time Debbie’s boyfriend ignored her, these schemas fired up, and she started working overtime to get his approval.

And viewed through the parts-based lens of Internal Family Systems (IFS), the part of Debbie that felt so defective and worthless was Little Debbie, who held all the painful feelings, memories, and ways of thinking from the years of being hurt by her alcohol-befuddled, cruel mother. When this part got triggered, a protective part then sprang into action to try and build her fragile self-esteem with any kind of compliment, praise, or approval she could muster. Debbie called this her “Love Me” part because, ultimately, that's what she needed, as we all do: to be seen and loved.

Learning to Love Herself

Over time, we worked with these and other parts, especially her inner critic whose harsh, devaluing messaging kept Debbie feeling bad about herself. And we also focused on helping her realize that no amount of external praise or validation would heal the wounds of childhood. The more her Love Me part sought it out, the more people got frustrated with Debbie and turned away, so it was counterproductive. Instead, Debbie learned to validate herself, which in IFS terminology means helping her self—the warm, compassionate inner resource we all possess—connect with, love, and reassure Little Debbie.

This internal validation was not only infinite, because her self was available 24/7 whenever Little Debbie felt bad, but it was also rock-solid. What I have learned from helping hundreds of clients is that, unlike the fragile nature of external validation, we can always validate ourselves. This becomes a kind of healing habit, because if we do it enough, it becomes automatic whenever we feel bad.

Debbie went on to find another boyfriend, who was much more interested and rarely on his phone. She also got a new job, and her sense of worth gradually increased until she was a happy, contented young woman.

If you’re interested in learning about how schema therapy, IFS, and other trauma-informed models can help you feel stronger and more worthy, my new book, Heal Your Trauma: How to Overcome a Painful Childhood to Become Happy and Whole Again, provides a step-by-step guide to healing. I very much hope you enjoy it.

*All case studies in these posts are composites; I never tell the stories of real clients, as confidentiality is very important to me.

item.title: Individual Sessions in Couples Therapy: What to Expect
item.description:
Therapy

Individual Sessions in Couples Therapy: What to Expect

How couples therapists balance individual privacy with couples treatment.

Posted October 14, 2026

Key points
  • Individual sessions can help couples therapists better understand each partner and support treatment progress.
  • Individual sessions may also occur to explore symptoms, build skills, or prepare for difficult conversations.
  • No-secrets policies address how therapists handle information that directly impacts couples treatment.
  • Therapists must balance individual privacy with the safety, ethics, and integrity of couples therapy.

Couples therapy usually involves partners meeting conjointly with a therapist, in person or via telehealth, to discuss relationship concerns. But individual appointments with the couples therapist can also be part of effective relational treatment. These meetings can help therapists better understand relationship dynamics, address barriers to progress, and support each partner’s therapeutic work.

Source: SHVETS production / Pexels

They also raise an important question: What happens when a client shares personal information during an individual session they have not yet shared with their partner?

Reasons for Individual Sessions During Couples Therapy

For many couples therapists, individual appointments are part of a structured intake process. One example is the 4-session evaluation model, which includes an initial conjoint session, followed by individual sessions with each partner, and concludes with a conjoint session focused on feedback and treatment planning.

Individual intakes can build client-therapist rapport and allow clients to speak more openly about their personal history, including early childhood experiences and family dynamics, previous relationships, and their perspective on current relationship issues. Individual intakes also allow the couples therapist to assess for safety concerns, such as active relational violence, which could indicate that couples therapy is not appropriate. Other factors, such as psychiatric issues and/or substance use, can also be evaluated that would warrant additional services or referrals.

Individual appointments may also occur throughout treatment. The purpose of these meetings includes addressing symptoms interfering with relational progress, targeting skills related to couples therapy goals, or preparing for a challenging conversation.

Are Individual Couples Therapy Sessions Kept Confidential?

Ultimately, in couples therapy, the "client" is the relationship, not any one person within it. Individual sessions aim to support progress toward the couple’s treatment goals. An individual appointment during couples treatment does not automatically mean the therapist has shifted into providing individual therapy. As such, individual sessions during couples therapy involve unique confidentiality considerations.

Source: SHVETS production / Pexels

Couples therapists have policies for managing information from individual sessions based on their professional codes of ethics and clinical best-practice guidelines. If you’re in couples therapy, your therapists should explain in advance how they handle individual disclosures, what confidentiality protections apply, and how information relevant to couples treatment may affect ongoing work.

The American Association for Marriage & Family Therapists (AAMFT) Code of Ethics states that a couples therapist “must not reveal any individual’s confidences to others in the client unit without the prior written permission of that individual.” Some couples therapists, though, utilize a no-secrets policy to manage disclosures and confidentiality. Such policies generally address how the therapist will respond when a partner privately discloses information that materially impacts the relationship or the goals of treatment.

It is important to understand how the AAMFT code described above interacts with these policies. If a couples therapist has a no-secrets policy, it means they reserve the right to refuse to keep a client's secret if it impedes their ability to help the couple. However, the AAMFT code still prevents the therapist from directly sharing that secret with the other partner without consent. Importantly, not all information shared in individual sessions is treated equally.

For example, a partner might disclose within an individual session an experience, such as childhood abuse, that they are not yet ready to share with their partner. If the information does not directly impact the direction of couples therapy, it does not automatically need to be shared. Instead, the couples therapist will discuss whether and how this information is relevant to the couples treatment, how you want your partner involved, and how they can support future discussions.

Source: SHVETS production / Pexels

The situation is different, however, when a partner reveals information that directly affects couples therapy and keeping it concealed would undermine the goals or integrity of treatment. A common example is if one partner privately discloses an ongoing affair. A no-secrets policy does not, by itself, authorize the therapist to reveal the affair. Instead, the therapist can explore reasons for nondisclosure, discuss the implications for treatment, and help the client consider how to disclose the information appropriately.

If the client refuses disclosure and the therapist cannot ethically or clinically continue conjoint treatment under the circumstances, the therapist may need to end couples therapy and/or offer a referral.

Why Individual Sessions Matter in Couples Therapy

In general, individual sessions can provide a valuable space for alliance building, assessment, personal reflection, and targeted therapeutic work to support your relationship. At the same time, couples therapists must balance respect for each partner’s privacy with responsibility for the treatment as a whole. Privacy is allowed; therapeutic collusion in maintaining secrets is not. Partners deserve space to work through personal experiences, while therapists must also protect the integrity, safety, and clinical purpose of couples treatment.

item.title: What Korean Can Teach Us About Envy
item.description:
Cross-Cultural Psychology

What Korean Can Teach Us About Envy

Comparison isn’t the thief of joy. Having only one word for envy might be.

Posted October 14, 2026

Key points
  • Envy is a universal emotion.
  • English speakers have only one word for envy; Koreans (and other cultures) have two.
  • Negative emotions are trying to tell you something important.

Have you ever watched a relative, friend, or colleague move forward while you're still figuring things out?

It's unsettling. Even if you are happy for them, you might have felt a pang in your gut. Or maybe you heard a little voice whispering, "Uh oh, you're falling behind!"

Maybe a classmate landed the kind of job you wanted. Or a cousin moved into a sweet new place. Maybe a coworker just announced a career change you've been quietly considering.

I am very familiar with this yuckiness. I admit I encounter this sensation all the time. It happens when I'm talking to a dear friend, catching up with an acquaintance, and scrolling through LinkedIn or Instagram. Even though I work with conscientious high achievers on how to build authentic confidence, it doesn't mean my confidence can't still shatter. Even though I've studied envy for the last five years, it doesn't mean I don't feel it.

Envy is a universal emotion, but we lack words

We all feel envy. We see something that someone else has, and it doesn't feel good. That's natural.

If you're thinking, "I don't envy." "I am not an envious person." I don’t need this article. Stick with me just a bit longer.

English speakers are more likely to deny or suppress this negative emotion not only because it doesn't feel good but because they don't have two distinct words for envy, as other cultures do. In Korean, for example, there is 부러움 (BOO-ruh-oom) and 시기 (SHEE-gee). These align with the two types of envy social science researchers call "benign" and "malicious." Koreans more freely express their benign envy, saying "부러워요" (BOO-ruh-wuh-yo) to elders, or "부럽다" (BOO-rup-da) to peers. It's a combination of "I envy you," I wish to be like you," and "I admire you."

These expressions become conversation starters. Recipients of such admissions are likely to respond by saying, "You can do what I did. Here is how." Or, when expressing gratitude, "I couldn't have done it if it were not for my team!"

English speakers also confuse envy with a similar but different emotion, jealousy. Jealousy is the fear of losing an important relationship to someone else. It requires three parties. For example, consider someone (1st party) who fears that his boss (2nd party) is enamored with the new hire's talent (3rd party), when he used to be her favorite employee and go-to person.

Envy, on the other hand, is simply wanting what someone else has. If you're preoccupied with the person who has what you want, maybe you wish he hadn’t gotten it, or you wish you could take that person down a notch, then you are experiencing "malicious" envy. Most people I meet are not malicious.

If you can direct your attention toward what it is that you want and away from the person who has it, then your envy is benign. It can be motivating.

Comparison is not the thief of joy

Another reason why envy gets a bad rap may be because we're told we shouldn't compare ourselves with other people. However, we're wired to compare! We are social beings; we can't help but look at others to figure out how to behave, how to join groups, how not to get kicked out. We look to others to figure out who we are.

But when we compare, we're likely to pay more attention to when we fall short. And this is where it doesn't feel good. There is discomfort, pain, and annoyance. And then, because we're told not to make social comparisons, we feel guilt and sometimes even shame.

As with many negative emotions, envy is trying to tell you something important. Negative emotions like stress, fear, anger, and envy, in moderation, are tools. They're alarm bells. Anger often points to injustice. Fear points to danger. Envy reveals what we want, who we might emulate, and where to start.

So what can we do?

I've learned that if we examine our envy, it not only defuses the discomfort, but we can learn something useful for our careers and relationships. But this requires looking more closely at what our envy tells us, going beyond the tangible and considering the intangible feelings we desire. If we do this, we can use our envy to find meaningful work and deepen relationships. This is what I hope to share in this column. Stay tuned for more specifics in the next post.

item.title: An Approach to Traumatic Brain Injury
item.description:
Traumatic Brain Injury

An Approach to Traumatic Brain Injury

Low-dose lithium for TBIs is a legitimate option.

Posted October 14, 2026

Key points
  • Healing depends on many factors, including chronic inflammation and neuroplasticity.
  • Low-dose nutritional lithium orotate is an emerging therapy.
  • Individualized treatment is the most effective.
Source: peterschreiber.media / Stock photo ID:1927703857

Traumatic brain injury is a lot more common than you might think. According to a recent survey from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, up to 29 percent of American adults report having a concussion or TBI at some point in their lives. That’s one in five of us. Among children and adolescents, the incidence is one in 10.

Of course, symptoms of TBI depend on injury severity. Common symptoms include headache, dizziness, fatigue, sleep problems, difficulty concentrating, and changes in mood and behavior.

To heal, we can reduce inflammation and cellular stress; support mitochondrial function—the energy generators inside your neurons; ensure healthy signaling between neurons; boost neuroplasticity—the brain's natural ability to repair, adapt, and regenerate.

Low-dose lithium is a therapeutic agent that can address all these issues in healing. While lithium is best-known as a pharmaceutical for bipolar disorder, it is also a trace mineral found naturally in low amounts in soil, water, and some foods. At these nutritional doses, research shows lithium can help reduce inflammation, improve mitochondrial function, and restore neuroplasticity. (For more on low-dose nutritional lithium orotate, please see my blog, Nutritional Lithium Orotate: A Mineral for Better Mood and Memory.)

Regulating Inflammation

Inflammation is one of the body’s first responses to injury. After a TBI, microglia—immune cells in the brain—activate, remove damaged tissue, coordinate the healing response, and support recovery. This acute inflammatory response is critical for healing.

The problems arise when this acute response becomes chronic. And that’s not uncommon. After a TBI, the blood-brain barrier—the protective system that supports and regulates communication between the brain and the rest of the body—may become more permeable, allowing inflammatory signals from outside the brain to more easily affect the brain, prolonging the inflammatory response. Inflammation can damage neurons and perpetuate symptoms. Low-dose lithium can promote a more balanced inflammatory response and protect neurons.

Protecting Mitochondria

After TBI, neurons may enter a state of metabolic stress; energy demands elevate, but energy production becomes less efficient. It’s the mitochondria—tiny organelles within each neuron—that are responsible for generating ATP, the primary form of cellular energy. But mitochondria are compromised by TBI.

Low-dose nutritional lithium helps preserve and support mitochondrial function, promoting cellular energy production. This reliable energy supports neuron-to-neuron communication and neuronal repair.

Strengthening Neuroplasticity

Recovery relies on neuroplasticity, which is the brain's natural ability to adapt and rewire itself. Several key mechanisms are at work:
reinforcing existing pathways between active brain cells; restructuring the microscopic junctions where neurons communicate; rebuilding and shifting the neural teams that handle specific tasks; producing brain-derived neurotrophic factor, a vital protein that maintains and grows healthy neurons.

Cellular and laboratory research shows that lithium can improve neuroplasticity, perhaps through regulating GSK-3, a key enzyme in brain activity.

Source: AmnajKhetsamtip / Stock photo ID:2286754354

The Hill Framework

Building on decades of research examining lithium’s biological effects on the brain, researchers have recently proposed the head impact—inflammation—low-dose lithium (Hill) framework as a model for understanding how inflammatory and metabolic responses following head injury may influence recovery. And how low-dose lithium might help.

The framework’s primary thesis: The mechanical impact initiates the injury, but the biological response that follows plays a central role in shaping recovery. Neuroinflammation, oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, impaired energy production, blood-brain barrier disruption, and altered neuroplasticity— these interact throughout the healing process, influencing both recovery and long-term neurological health.

The framework proposes that low-dose lithium addresses many aspects of this biological response. It doesn’t suggest that lithium is the treatment for TBI. Rather, it explores whether influencing the recovery pathways with low-dose lithium may create a more favorable environment for healing—using multiple modalities, including physical rehabilitation, cognitive-behavioral therapy, and repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation, to name a few.

Individualized Recovery

I am a functional psychiatrist, and a key tenet of my approach to any condition—including TBI—is taking into account the individual’s biological parameters, all of which influence the brain’s capacity to adapt and recover. While the initial injury may be similar, recovery is highly individualized, shaped by the interactions of multiple bodily systems—the nervous system, the cardiovascular system, the hormonal system, and others.

Recovery extends beyond cognitive symptoms like memory loss and difficulty concentrating. Persistent headaches, dizziness, sleep disturbances, fatigue, anxiety, mood changes, digestive symptoms, and more may be part of an individual’s situation. For maximum effectiveness, the clinician and patient need to recognize the distinct post-injury picture—and treat it accordingly.

Source: Maglara / Stock photo ID:1198868597

Ideally, these treatments include:

  • Nutrition, providing the building blocks for neurological repair and adaptation
  • Gut health, to positively influence chronic, systemic inflammation
  • Sleep, to provide a period for restoring energy and clearing metabolic waste
  • Stress regulation, with less stress reducing inflammation and improving sleep

In this context, low-dose lithium is one emerging therapy within a comprehensive, individualized approach to recovery from TBI. The philosophy: Use every effective means available to support the brain’s natural capacity to heal. The Hill framework reflects this evolving understanding.

item.title: The Question Psychiatry Never Asked
item.description:
Psychiatry

The Question Psychiatry Never Asked

Privacy law may close a clinician’s mouth. Nothing requires closing their ears.

Posted October 14, 2026

Key points
  • HIPAA does not stop clinicians from listening to families, but many avoid it for fear of breaking the law.
  • Families can help by writing down what they observe and asking clinicians for a chance to share it.
  • Clinicians can start with one question for families: What was this person like before the illness?
Source: Kristin Hardwick/StockSnap

After driving through the night, my mother arrived at the ICU at three in the morning to find me, her youngest son, intubated and in a medically induced coma after my fourth suicide attempt in nine weeks. On the whiteboard, my medical team had written my name as “Pat.” She erased it and wrote “Patrick,” as I had never been a Pat. “It angered me that they made assumptions about the person lying in that bed,” she later reflected, “about the person who they did not want to know.”

What my mother carried into that ICU room has a name in clinical practice: collateral history. And across 10 years of my untreated bipolar I disorder, only one clinician, an intensivist, asked my family for it, and it was in the context of whether to withdraw life support. No psychiatrist inquired about it to understand the origins and contours of my psychological suffering—a reality of family exclusion that is far too common in our system, where the patient is treated as the sole source of information about himself.

Collateral history is vital information from those who intimately know the patient, gathered to complete or correct what the patient reports. Federal guidelines state clearly that HIPAA “in no way prevents health care providers from listening to family members or other caregivers.” Many clinicians, however, shy away from soliciting it out of fear they are violating privacy laws.

The remedy is to be found in a change of practice. As one member of the Nova Scotia Moms, a Canadian advocacy group, put it, a clinician’s mouth may be closed to protect a patient’s privacy, but their ears should be open to hearing what a patient can’t always see.

Throughout my decade of despair, I was blind to my own illness due to a neurological lack of insight called anosognosia. My family had knowledge that should have been integrated into my care. It was my mother—not any of my psychiatrists—who kept asking the right questions about the roots of my psychic pain. She kept wondering where my anxiety was coming from, a question that might have led someone curious to the brain infection no one was testing for. For psychiatrists, ever since the advent of psychiatry’s bible in the DSM-III in 1980, as anthropologist Tanya Luhrmann has noted, “it did not matter how a patient had become depressed or why.”

My cousin, too, accurately floated the possibility that I had a bipolar disorder—the same illness another cousin had—four years before any clinician ever diagnosed it. She was never brought into the conversation.

When my mother asked to be included in my psychiatric assessment after my stint in the ICU, she was told she could not because of privacy laws. Two weeks later, however, I was discharged into her care. She was deemed sufficient to care for me but incapable of learning the full scope of what she was caring for.

Almost a decade later, when I was a patient at a state psychiatric hospital, the pattern of unasked questions continued. Only once my mother pressed my care team on a number of fronts did they schedule one conference call and dutifully answer all of her questions. But when she asked if she could be involved in my therapy and recovery, even after I signed a release form, the response was “we have no mechanism for that.”

Source: Pavel Danilyuk/Pexels

Collateral history supplies a missing perspective. When someone can’t see through the smog of their sickness, the family’s account of who they were before is often the only way to distinguish the person from the illness. A psychiatrist in a 15-minute appointment sees a snapshot, while my mother recorded a disturbing constellation of behaviors in her journal across a quarter of my life.

“Patrick is slipping once again,” she wrote, “didn’t go to work; isn’t responding; is sending hateful messages. I’ve seen the pattern before.” In 2020, she reread her entries from 2017 and “saw the same manic escalation repeating.” She regularly read the acceleration in my syntax before the arrival of the full manic crisis, and she could have shared her impressions of these outbreaks if anyone had asked. She did not know she could offer them.

While my mother’s journal was a form of self-care, it could also have served as critical data that informed my treatment. The philosopher Miranda Fricker calls it testimonial injustice when prejudice leads a listener to give a speaker’s word “a deflated level of credibility.” In mental health care, families know this phenomenon all too well: clinicians commonly assume that a frightened parent is too emotional to be a reliable witness. When filed as worry rather than weighed as evidence, collateral history becomes the absent half of the record.

As critics warn, the charge of lack of insight can be used to dismiss a patient’s wishes. Families can be part of the problem, and they should not overrule patient autonomy if the patient has reasonable objections to an intervention. Families that have been on the receiving end of the manic cruelty I described in this post may be reluctant to share knowledge out of fear of retaliation. In such cases, families can ask that what they reveal be kept confidential, and federal rules allow it to be withheld if the patient later requests his records, sparing them the “fear of disrupting the family’s relationship with the patient.”

To foster a culture of collateral history in mental health care, families and clinicians can both play a role. Families should document as much as they can about a loved one’s case, even when no one is asking yet. They should push for meetings with clinicians to convey essential information about a patient—including a request to keep information private, if necessary. If a clinician won’t listen, they can reach out to a patient representative department. For their part, clinicians can ask family members a simple question: “Tell me about this person. What were they like before the illness?”

That was the culture of curiosity and compassionate care that my mother was trying to model when she erased the word “Pat” from the ICU whiteboard and wrote “Patrick.” As she later described it in her journal, my mother confronted the nurse who was tending to me without a word and reminded her: “He is not just another suicide attempt. He is my son.” Collateral history asks clinicians to make that correction themselves, as a matter of routine, before a mother has to drive through the night to make it for them.

item.title: When You Ask 'Who Am I?' Forgiving Can Change Your Identity
item.description:
Forgiveness

When You Ask 'Who Am I?' Forgiving Can Change Your Identity

A negative identity from suffering can be reversible when you forgive..

Posted October 14, 2026

Key points
  • Answering "Who am I?" gets complicated when struggling with emotional wounds.
  • Without a clear plan for altering a negative identity, it can settle into a consistent pattern of defeatism.
  • Forgiving can address the emotional wounds and also begin to change one's identity more positively.
Source: Fizkes / Dreamstime

Having studied forgiveness for over 40 years, I am saddened that injustices—and the pain and suffering—alter a person's identity. One indication is a consistent finding of low self-esteem in those who were treated badly (see, for example, Lin and team, 2004; Reed and Enright, 2006). If one's identity is not consistently established in adolescence (Erik Erikson 1968, 1994), then it is easier to slip into identity confusion, or a lack of consistency in answering the question, "Who am I?" If some people's identity is not firm, consistent, and fair in how they treat others and themselves, that identity can become distorted, often to the detriment of those who were treated unfairly. Low scores on forgiveness and self-esteem scales are signs that unjust treatment has damaged identity.

A central question: When people are treated deeply unjustly and begin to dislike even themselves, how can they establish a more wholesome, adaptive identity? Forgiving others accurately can establish or even re-establish an adaptive, healthy identity. Here are six ideas to consider. Before turning to these six ideas, take a moment to understand what forgiving others "accurately" is. According to a recent philosophical analysis (Song, Enright, and Kim, 2025), forgiveness is the moral virtue of deliberately being good to those who have not been good to you and following through on this. It takes time, often more than 12 weeks of work (Baskin and Enright, 2004), and it focuses on the offending person, not the self—you. The paradox is that, as people extend mercy to offenders, scientific studies show forgivers experience psychological benefits.

1. The other has inherent worth. I have inherent worth.

In our process model of forgiveness (Enright and Fitzgibbons, 2024), forgiving often begins with thinking about the one who offended, particularly by expanding one's view of this person. The forgiver is encouraged to see the other person's emotional wounds, not to excuse what happened, but to see a vulnerable person who has been hurt and is passing on those wounds to you. Further, the forgiver is encouraged to think of how the other person and the self share a common humanity; both need good nutrition, good rest, and good relationships. The point is to expand one's vision of offending others to see their inherent worth as persons. They are more than their unjust actions. As forgivers, over time, widen their vision of who the offenders are, the forgivers also tend to begin offering this inherent worth to the self: "There is more to me than the wounds I have suffered. I, too, possess worth that cannot be taken from me." We see the fruit of this in the positively changed self-esteem scores discussed above.

2. It takes courage to forgive; I am growing in courage

Source: Photographerlondon / Dreamstime

In our process model of forgiveness, once forgivers have an open view of offenders—seeing their inherent worth—we ask them, when they are ready, to stand in the pain of what happened. This is not to disavow what happened, but to become a conduit of good toward them so forgivers do not keep throwing the pain back at the offenders or unsuspecting others. To stand in this pain requires courage because it is not easy to resist getting back at the offenders. A new insight can now emerge: I am not a weakling, as the nineteenth-century philosopher Nietzsche asserted, if I can stand strong and avoid revenge (1887/1989). Identity begins to shift when seeing oneself as courageous rather than as someone devastated by the offense(s).

3. I am not dominated by the power of others

As forgivers begin to see their anger diminishing, their self-esteem rising, and their gradual release from the torment of inner negative emotions, they have the insight that the offending ones no longer have power over them. After all, they no longer carry the daily negative thoughts, feelings, and even behaviors that emerged as effects of the injustice(s). Instead, and this can be surprising, they have greater quiet, which may not have occurred for a long time.

4. I have suffered; I can see many people’s suffering now

As people suffer from unjust treatment, they often gain insight into the burdens many others carry. For example, forgivers might be more attentive to co-workers having a bad day, or to a partner who was treated unfairly by certain family members when growing up. The forgiver can see more clearly into another's heart.

5. I know how to give good gifts

Forgiveness changes your character; it turns patience, compassion, and mercy from hard-won exceptions into a natural way to treat people. You become a conduit of goodness and love toward others, including patience with a partner or spending more time with one's children. As one example, a man within a correctional institution told me that even though he is imprisoned for life, his new goal is to help his cellmates forgive. It enlivened him with a positive new purpose, even behind the prison walls.

6. I am a thriver, not just a survivor.

Source: Dark1elf / Dreamstime

As one person stated, after forgiving, she had settled on an identity of victim, and she lived that out with bitterness. Eventually, she began to see herself as a survivor as her anger and anxiety diminished. Later, she changed her identity and now sees herself as a thriver. We can see this in our research, in which abused women reported having more command over challenging situations in life and handling responsibilities well (Reed and Enright, 2007).

Who am I?

In summary, when people forgive accurately and take enough time, their identities change for the better. They tend to acknowledge their inherent worth, develop more courage, own their inner world, aid others in their struggles, practice gift-giving, and begin to thrive in life. Have you been deeply hurt by others' injustices? Who are you as a person? As you forgive, your identity may change for the better.

item.title: The Two Most Overlooked Causes of Addiction
item.description:
Addiction

The Two Most Overlooked Causes of Addiction

What addiction may be trying to do for us

Posted October 14, 2026

Key points
  • Addiction may begin as an attempt to soothe unmet needs for connection and relief from pain.
  • Loneliness and substance misuse can reinforce each other, deepening disconnection.
  • Recovery isn't based on willpower alone; it can require healing unresolved pain and building safe connections.

Nearly half of U.S. adults showed problematic signs of at least one addiction in a given year. That was the finding of a 2011 study by Sussman, Lisha, and Griffiths. It predates the smartphone era, engagement-optimized algorithms, and legalized sports betting. I suspect the number has only grown. Epic Research (2026) found that diagnosed gambling disorder rose more than 60 percent in states that legalized sports betting since 2018, while it fell in states that did not.

So why is addiction so widespread?

Genetics gets much of the attention. While some people do inherit a nervous system more vulnerable to addiction, vulnerability isn’t destiny. What happens in our relationships and environments powerfully shapes whether that vulnerability develops into addiction.

Most of my clients struggling with addiction tell me that they want to stop but don’t know how. One client turns to whiskey, especially when stressors involving his children, partner, and work begin to collide, even though he knows it compromises his sleep, marriage, health, and ability to focus. We’ve been working together on learning to turn toward other people for support rather than whiskey. That shift gets at something I believe is central to understanding addiction.

As Gabor Maté has suggested, perhaps the more useful question isn’t simply why the addiction, but why the pain behind it? What is the addiction doing for the person? What is it helping them escape or relieve? I believe the answers to these questions bring us closer to its roots.

After 15 years in this work, I’ve often seen addiction begin as an attempt to fulfill two deeply intertwined needs. By the time someone seeks help, that attempted solution has become a serious problem of its own. Understanding what drew them toward it can help us see what’s actually missing.

Root one: disconnection

This isn’t always one isolated in a basement. Sometimes it’s the executive who has 30 Teams channels open but zero people he’d feel comfortable reaching out to, and limited people who’d show up for him if he called in a pinch. I’ve come to see addiction as less exclusively a chemistry problem and more a relationship problem, often wearing a brain-chemistry costume. The substance, the scroll, the cake, the bet—they’re reliable. People, unfortunately, are far more complicated, but also far more substantive. They require trust, investment, and reciprocity. They can’t always be counted on to show up when we need them. That reliability must be built long-term, through trust and investment in the relationship—to me, that’s the defining difference.

The research backs up what I’ve seen in my sessions. The brain’s opioid system regulates social bonding, and social disconnection isn’t just a side effect of addiction but may also help drive it (Løseth et al., 2025). The relationship can become self-reinforcing: disconnection can increase substance use, while substance use can further erode relationships. Morris and Onyegesi (2025) similarly described loneliness and substance misuse as a self-reinforcing loop in young adults and proposed an attachment-based practice model. Kurt and Taşdemir (2026) found that insecure attachment and emotional neglect were associated with separation anxiety among people with substance use disorder, while secure attachment appeared to buffer the effects of neglect.

The pandemic gave us an unsettling natural experiment: as much of the world became sharply more socially isolated, drug-related deaths rose sharply in many places. By contrast, places that maintained more social continuity (like Sweden), which took a markedly different approach to lockdowns, did not see the same increase. That doesn’t prove isolation caused the difference, but it’s hard not to notice the relationship.

Part of root one is at least one absent attachment. I say “at least one” deliberately. Without indicting one’s childhood, we can still notice where it often originates. If no one modeled “I can be upset, and you’ll still stay,” one grows up needing something that will stay predictably regulated no matter what they bring to it. A substance or addictive behavior doesn’t get its feelings hurt or need you to read the room. That’s a nervous system often doing the best it can to get the comfort and nurturance it needed to survive with the relationships (or lack thereof) it was handed.

And these patterns don’t always begin with the person who eventually develops the addiction. They’re often embedded in families long before one becomes addicted (Juhnke & Hagedorn, 2019). The addiction is often what is labeled, but the underlying patterns, what EFT recognizes as an adaptive response to an unmet need for connection, were inherited long before. Without a safe connection to help process difficult experiences, emotional pain usually gets trapped inside the body, setting the stage for the second root.

Root two: unprocessed or unhealed pain or trauma

I’ve repeatedly seen how experiences from years or even decades earlier continue to shape how people cope with distress. I’m not necessarily referring to major, unambiguously catastrophic events like an earthquake, physical abuse, or a car crash. Trauma is less about the event than the body’s reaction to it. Sometimes it’s the accumulation of a thousand small moments where one learned that needing something from others was dangerous or pointless. The nervous system remembers.

Suppressing trauma intrusions demands so much mental energy that the exhaustion itself can push people toward addiction for relief. This is where EMDR excels in my practice, not by arguing someone out of a coping mechanism but by reprocessing what it got stuck on decades before addiction emerged, usually as a coping mechanism initially.

The numbers point the same way. Azagba et al. (2025) found a dose-response relationship among U.S. high school students: more adverse childhood experiences (ACEs) meant more addiction. Mongan et al. (2025) followed a population-based sample into early adulthood and found that parent and peer relationship quality and school engagement mediated how childhood adversity led to substance use later on.

So to me, an emerging addiction equation may be: disconnection + difficulty regulating painful internal states = addictive (substance and/or behavior) as relief.

None of this excuses the wreckage addiction leaves behind. A cough can be “just a symptom” of a cold and still keep the whole house up at night. But if we only ever treat the cough, we miss the infection, and eventually we’re band-aiding the same cough again.

Connection is thus the underrated engine of prevention. If addiction often starts as a way to survive disconnection (Hari, 2015), then the antidote can’t be willpower alone. It was always going to be a person, or several, who could carry one’s heavy emotion with them without flinching. To me, this largely explains why therapists have jobs. Relationships contribute to wounds, and relationships are thus part of how we heal.

I’m not saying every addiction begins with loneliness or trauma. Addiction has many contributing causes. But in my clinical work, disconnection and unresolved pain have been two of the most consistently overlooked pieces of the puzzle. Recovery can involve more than white-knuckling our way through cravings; it can mean finding people we no longer have to struggle alone with.

Relationships can offer something that stopping alone cannot. Beyond sobriety, there’s the work of building the human connections that addiction may have helped us endure living without.

item.title: My Experience Quitting Alcohol
item.description:
Alcoholism

My Experience Quitting Alcohol

Personal Perspective: Older adults who stop drinking may experience odd symptoms

Posted October 14, 2026

Key points
  • A 2025 Gallup survey found that 54 percent of adults consume alcohol.
  • The research on moderate alcohol consumption has shifted from positive to negative outcomes.
  • Responses after stopping moderate consumption vary in individuals but may be more profound in older adults.
  • Older adults who quit for health reasons are labeled sick quitters rather than abstainers or non-drinkers.

In August 2023, my cardiologist strongly suggested that alcohol may be causing an irregular heart rhythm. I didn’t read the summary until I saw him the day before my 2024 appointment. That was the beginning of my life without alcohol. On June 6, 2024, I stopped consuming alcohol. I assumed that the cessation would be a simple process.

A 2025 Gallup survey found that 54 percent of U.S. adults 18 and older who consume alcohol say they had an average of 3.2 drinks over the past week. These rates were way down from the peak of 71 percent of self-reported drinkers in 1976, 1977, and 1978.

Retirement and Losses

A phenomenon known as sudden retirement syndrome refers to the feelings of being lost, purposeless, or adrift after retiring from one’s career. For many people, their job isn’t just a means to earn a living; it’s a central aspect of their identity and purpose. When that role ends, many may feel lost.

Leaving work can strip away your sense of purpose and self-worth. No longer do you reap the financial rewards and achievements that a job provided.

Physical and Psychological Symptoms

Within 24 hours of abstinence, the nighttime awakening began with a nonspecific state of anxiety. At times, I was unable to catch my breath. Leaving the bedroom and going to another room to listen to calming music would allow me to relax.

On day two of post-cessation, I began walking multiple loops in the hallways of our condo building. The building takes up an entire square block. This pattern continued with anxiety attacks in an on-off pattern for the next two weeks.

Then, in the fifth week of abstinence, a long-term friend of 20-plus years and I had a falling out initiated by him. I was distressed over this sudden rejection. I experienced a significant and alarming spike in my BP that morning. After 3.5 laps around the building, the next morning, my BP was within normal limits. I began grieving the loss of our friendship.

Anxiety or Panic Attacks

Within five weeks, I lost seven pounds and was excited. However, I was losing entire nights of sleep from anxiety attacks. These physical symptoms persisted for a couple of weeks. I was unable to sleep in bed with my partner and would sit in a chair in the living room all night and try to sleep without much success.

My anxiety and panic attacks continued intermittently for six weeks and gradually stopped. During those long weeks of withdrawal, I often slept in the living room in a chair and continued my daily walking schedule to moderate anxiety.

Undiagnosed Anxiety Disorder?

Being an academic and nurse practitioner, I began to realize I probably have an anxiety disorder. I began searching for information. While anxiety disorders are treatable, less than half of those affected receive treatment. Physicians and health care providers often prescribe anti-anxiety medications.

The drugs supposedly have a low potential for abuse and low risk of dependence. Examples of these popular prescription drugs include alprazolam and diazepam. Due to their ability to produce feelings of intense relaxation, sedation, and anxiety relief, they often lead to lifelong dependence.

Anxiety and Alcohol Use

Alcohol withdrawal may have unleashed an anxiety disorder that was preexisting or being masked. However, alcohol withdrawal also leads to temporary symptoms of anxiety.

As someone goes through withdrawal, they may experience high levels of anxiety. This is usually the result of the increased sensitivity that the body displays when it has stopped drinking. Anxiety can be so severe that people feel as though they are on edge, and they may also have difficulties sleeping as a result.

It’s not uncommon to experience a range of disturbing symptoms, including anxiety. It’s even more common to find that after you’ve stopped drinking, anxiety makes you want to go back to alcohol.

The New Scientific Consensus

Older studies of alcohol consumption were flawed. Researchers classified participants as abstainers or non-drinkers; however, many were older adults who quit drinking for health reasons. This group was labeled as the “sick quitter effect.”

The recategorizing of active moderate drinkers from sick former drinkers demonstrated no protective benefits from moderate alcohol consumption. The findings lead to a high incidence of multiple types of cancer with minimal cardiovascular benefit.

Conclusion

As nonalcoholic alternatives to alcoholic beverages become more common, Gallup added a survey question this year and found that 17 percent of Americans—20 percent of drinkers and 14 percent of non-drinkers—have chosen a nonalcoholic beer, wine, or spirits over an alcoholic drink in the past year.

I do miss occasional glasses of wine and favorite cocktails, but I don’t miss the withdrawal experiences. The restaurant industry and wine producers have quickly adapted to the new, healthy lifestyle without alcohol.

The various mocktails and nonalcoholic beers have become my favorite substitutes. As time moves on, I occasionally miss the feelings that were derived from alcohol, but I value my health, which is more important.

item.title: 'Sacred Flaws,' Cling to Them, or Change and Grow?
item.description:
Self-Sabotage

'Sacred Flaws,' Cling to Them, or Change and Grow?

"Sacred flaws" are ways of thinking and behaving that work—until they don’t.

Posted October 14, 2026

Key points
  • Will Storr, in 'The Science of Storytelling,' proposes the sacred flaw approach to writing fiction.
  • Sacred flaws are protagonists’ long-term ways of thinking and behaving that work well—until they don’t.
  • Storr’s sacred flaw approach offers vocabulary and metaphor for framing real people’s real-life struggles.
  • Is it better to cling to flawed ways of thinking and behaving or risk change and growth?

I was recently working with the parent of a young adult who has identified as autistic and transgender, ways of being in the world this parent struggles to understand and for which acceptance does not come easily. This parent is heroically striving to repair their strained relationship. They emailed this to me recently (quoted and lightly edited with permission):

I have been thinking about our conversation about changing a story we tell ourselves when it’s not working anymore. It helps me see why so much that my adult kids do shakes me to the core, even when it shouldn’t: all of it contravenes the narrative I keep trying to keep alive . . . a narrative that I didn’t even consciously embrace. . . It’s good to give it up. Freeing, I think.

“Changing the story we tell ourselves when it’s not working anymore,” “the narrative I keep trying to keep alive,” “a narrative that I didn’t even consciously embrace,” “It’s good to give it up”—versions of this way of thinking have, since early in my professional career, been an important part of my clinical work. It is consistent with multiple therapy orientations, such as cognitive therapy (changing “schema” or beliefs about self, others, or the world), as well as Buddhist practices and Stoic philosophies (e.g., giving up attachments, differentiating what one can control from what one can’t).

I have, more recently, found new metaphors and vocabulary for talking about these concepts in ways that seem to more immediately engage and even inspire patients such as this one. These new (to me) metaphors and vocabulary come from a book about reading and writing stories, Will Storr’s The Science of Storytelling, especially his discussions of “the sacred flaw approach.”

The Sacred Flaw Approach

I introduce patients to the sacred flaw approach using versions of this:

A respected colleague recommended a book to me a couple of years ago. The book is written by someone who teaches writing and is written for writers This book suggests that the protagonists, the main characters, in many if not most books, movies, and plays, here and in cultures around the world, can be seen as struggling to figure out what to do with their sacred flaw: a way of thinking about self, others, and the world; a pattern of behaving or interacting; life strategies; values and goals that were discovered and embraced early in life and worked well—were even “super powers” for years, perhaps got them through very challenging even traumatic times, perhaps resulted in successes and achievements—until something changes and it doesn’t work anymore. However, even though it has become “flawed,” they cling to it like it is a sacred object.

The book or movie or play is mostly about the protagonist’s struggles to give up the flaw—or not—and find an alternative way to be and to live—or not. We know that stories are similar in all cultures, all around the world. This likely means that basic plots tap into something universal about human lives and human psychology. In other words, all of us struggle, at some point in our lives, with sacred flaws. I am thinking, as we talk here today, that perhaps this sacred flaw approach might be a useful way to think about what you are struggling with and working on.

Storr coaches aspiring writers to think through the origin story of their character’s sacred flaw, most likely (though not always) from childhood or adolescence, and then consider how:

“As they grow up, your character’s flawed theory of control will build a particular life for them. It’ll lead them on a particular journey—into a particular job with a particular romantic history, into a particular neighborhood and a particular home with a particular front door with a particular color and state of repair. They’ll have particular values and particular friends and enemies and particular goals, obstacles, and fears.”

Storr adds that “Our protagonist’s sacred belief . . . was, at one point, her superpower. It helped earn her everything she most valued. It gave her confidence, tenacity, and courage.” It might have led to safety; material or career gains; a sense of heightened status, even superiority; friends, colleagues, or lovers; life goals; and beliefs about achievements that will make them happy or safe. It will also cause them to worry about what they risk losing if they act against their flaw and dread what will happen if they act against their flaw.

Then something changes in the story, to or around the character, that presents “an overwhelming challenge to their sacred flaw and ultimately break(s) it apart.” This could be (a partial list): an opportunity; a journey; an investigation; a misunderstanding; a discovery; a promotion or demotion; an enemy; an accusation; an onerous task; a dare or challenge; an injustice; a temptation; a betrayal.

Then their superpower becomes their downfall—or not, depending on whether they cling to it or change. Change is hard and feels and may be risky.

Storr writes that “Many of the most memorable characters in fiction, and reality, derive their fascination from the fact that they’re making a fundamental mistake about the human world and their place within it.”

He adds, “The standard five-act structure is simply the most efficient way of showing a character’s sacred flaw being tested, broken, and rebuilt” (emphasis added):

  • Act I: This is me, and it’s not working.
  • Act II: Is there another way?
  • Act III: There is. I have transformed.
  • Act IV: But can I handle the pain of change?
  • Act V: Who am I going to be?

The Sacred Flaw Approach and Therapy

In my mind, Storr’s sacred flaw approach fits with why people come to therapy (a life strategy, a change happens, it’s not working, what do I do about it?); differences between beginning and later stages of therapy (help me fix my strategy; get it to work again vs. help me find new strategies); and what people can get out of therapy (or other personal growth experiences)—more adaptive ways of thinking and behaving.

An Invitation

I invite you to think about this post in reference to your own life, perhaps especially if you are a neurodivergent adult or the parent of someone who is neurodivergent. Are the strategies that you creatively developed and wisely embraced to get through the many challenges of childhood and adolescence, and/or parenting, still working? If not, do the benefits of change make adapting worth it?
